findings.summary: The cancellation/timeout counterfactual has no independent cleanup fallback, so a regression can leak the gated tasks it is meant to prove are reaped.
findings.diagnosis: After creating the owner, facade, completion, and guard tasks, the test performs its waits and assertions without a try/finally. If complete_before_deadlock_guard regresses by failing to set release or terminate, the timeout assertion at lines 276-284 fails while release remains unset and some or all of those tasks remain pending. That reproduces the unbounded test-cleanup defect this follow-up is intended to close, so the negative test does not fail safely against the buggy implementation.
findings.evidence: Lines 270-287 create and inspect the guard with no finally block; by contrast, the early-lifecycle counterfactual at lines 243-245 unconditionally sets release and gathers its tasks after any assertion failure.
findings.correction: Wrap the cancellation/timeout exercise and assertions in a try/finally that always sets release, cancels any still-pending guard if necessary, and gathers owner, facade, completion, and guard with return_exceptions=True before leaving the test.

findings.summary: The cancellation case uses asyncio.sleep(0) as a scheduling readiness signal.
findings.diagnosis: A single event-loop yield assumes the guard has entered complete_before_deadlock_guard before guard.cancel() runs. That ordering is scheduler-dependent; an alternate loop policy may cancel the task before its cleanup body starts, producing a failure unrelated to the contract under test.
findings.evidence: The only synchronization before guard.cancel("offline caller cancellation") is await asyncio.sleep(0) at line 274.
findings.correction: Expose or instrument a deterministic event that is set after the guard enters its completion wait, await that event, and then cancel the guard.
